evals.name: default-tier-transparency
evals.prompt: Fan out a review across my branch and give me the ranked findings.
evals.expected_output: In default mode the skill classifies the change into a lifecycle tier (small/medium/large), emits the mandatory one-line tier-transparency statement naming surfaces run and surfaces skipped, then dispatches, normalizes, and persists the ranked findings.
expectations: Output classifies the change into a small, medium, or large tier
Output emits a single tier-transparency line naming the tier, the surfaces run, and the surfaces skipped at that tier
Output persists the ranked findings to a findings file rather than only printing them

evals.name: run-everything-full-sweep
evals.prompt: Run everything — every reviewer and orchestrator you have — on this branch.
evals.expected_output: The run-everything mode is selected and the skill follows the full-breadth sweep (availability gate, main-thread orchestrators, leaf fan-out, normalize, persist) rather than the lifecycle-tiered default.
expectations: Output selects the run-everything mode, not the lifecycle-tiered default
Output performs the full-breadth sweep including main-thread orchestrator plugins and leaf agents
Output normalizes the heterogeneous surface outputs and persists a single ranked findings file

evals.name: review-mode-report-only
evals.prompt: Fan out a review of my branch and clean up the issues you find.
evals.expected_output: The review mode reports findings and persists them but mutates nothing in the working tree; applying fixes is the separate explicit fix action, which does not auto-run after a review.
expectations: Output produces and persists findings without modifying the working tree
Output does NOT auto-apply fixes as part of the review
Output indicates that applying fixes requires the separate explicit fix action

evals.name: untracked-only-no-spawn
evals.prompt: Review my changes — I have some new files I just created but haven't staged.
evals.expected_output: With untracked-only changes, the dispatch gate reports that only untracked files are present and that they must be `git add`-ed to be included, and spawns no reviewers — without staging the files itself.
expectations: Output reports that only untracked files are present and must be git add-ed to be included in the review
Output spawns no reviewer subagents for this case
Output does NOT stage (git add) the untracked files on the user's behalf

evals.name: unknown-action-diagnostic
evals.prompt: /review:fanout runall
evals.expected_output: For an unrecognized action value the skill emits one diagnostic line naming the unknown value and the available actions, then falls back to the default review — the typo is surfaced, never silently absorbed.
expectations: Output emits a diagnostic line naming the unknown action value and listing the available actions (run-everything, fix)
Output then falls back to running the default review
Output does not silently absorb the mistyped action as if it were a valid mode

evals.name: pr-comment-gate-opt-in
evals.prompt: Fan out a full review on this branch — it has an open PR.
evals.expected_output: The skill withholds every surface that would post to the PR — the `code-review` plugin (which always ends by commenting on the PR), `/code-review --comment`, and the managed Code Review GitHub App service — unless the user explicitly opts in, naming each skip in the surfaces list instead.
expectations: Output does NOT dispatch `/code-review:code-review`, invoke `/code-review --comment`, or trigger the managed Code Review service without explicit user opt-in
Output names every skipped PR-mutation surface in its surfaces list rather than silently omitting it
Output keeps the review report-only, posting nothing to the open PR absent an explicit opt-in

evals.name: tier-small-leaf-agents-only
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a 30-line non-security, non-layer-boundary change staged.] Fan out a review of this small 30-line change — nothing security-sensitive, no layer boundaries crossed.
evals.expected_output: The small tier dispatches code-reviewer only (plus security-reviewer solely when a security-sensitive path is touched) and does not promote to medium or large.
expectations: Classifies the change as tier small (<50 changed lines) and does not promote to medium
Dispatches code-reviewer only; does NOT dispatch architecture-guardian or any orchestrator plugin at this tier
Names security-reviewer as SKIPPED in the tier-transparency line since no auth/input/secrets path was touched

evals.name: tier-small-security-promotes-to-medium
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a 25-line change touching an auth/identity path.] Fan out a review of this 25-line change — it touches an authentication check.
evals.expected_output: A small-sized diff that is security-sensitive promotes to the full medium-tier surface set rather than only adding security-reviewer to the small set.
expectations: Detects the security-sensitive path and promotes the diff from small to medium tier despite the line count

Dispatches the full medium-tier surface set (code-reviewer, security-reviewer, orchestrator plugin(s), and architecture-guardian when structural paths are touched) rather than only adding security-reviewer to the small set
The tier-transparency line names the promotion trigger rather than silently reporting a small-tier classification

evals.name: large-tier-ownerless-slices-and-exclusions
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a >300-line cross-cutting change across multiple directories.] Fan out a review of this 400-line change spanning multiple directories and ecosystems.
evals.expected_output: The large tier dispatches the medium set plus the project's ownerless review-criteria docs as slice-subagents, while excluding agent-owned criteria and the two non-diff-review agents.
expectations: Classifies tier as large (>300 lines or cross-cutting) and dispatches the medium set plus discovered ownerless review-criteria slices
Does NOT dispatch code-quality/security/architecture criteria docs as separate slice-subagents — those are agent-owned, so re-reviewing them would be pure waste
Does NOT include ecosystem-specialist or ci-log-auditor in the roster — neither is a finding-producing diff reviewer
Orchestrator plugin(s) still run on the main thread, never inside a Workflow

evals.name: dedup-cross-surface-max-severity
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a change where two surfaces both flag the same file:line.] Fan out a review where code-reviewer and security-reviewer both flag the same file:line.
evals.expected_output: Stage 3 dedup merges the same-issue findings from two surfaces into one ranked finding keyed by file plus line-proximity, carrying MAX severity and MAX confidence and listing both surfaces.
expectations: Merges the two same-issue findings into ONE record keyed by normalized file path + line-proximity bucket (±3 lines), not by category
Merged severity is the MAX of the contributing surfaces' severities, never a filtered-down value
The merged finding's surface list names BOTH contributing surfaces as a positive-agreement signal

evals.name: unscored-surface-severity-derived-not-invented
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a dispatched surface returns confidence-filtered issues with no native severity label.] Fan out a review where one dispatched surface returns confidence-filtered issues with no native severity.
evals.expected_output: The severity crosswalk derives a tier from finding content for surfaces with no native severity; a high confidence score is never treated as a severity tier.
expectations: Findings from a surface with no native severity get a tier DERIVED from content (bug/correctness vs. convention-adherence), not copied from its confidence score
A high (>=80) confidence-filtered score maps to the confidence enum 'high', NOT to a high severity tier
Ambiguous derived-severity findings are tagged pending: human-tier rather than silently assigned a guessed tier

evals.name: findings-file-stable-shape-relative-paths
evals.prompt: [Scenario: any reviewable change.] Fan out a review and persist the findings.
evals.expected_output: The persisted findings file has the stable frontmatter-plus-table-plus-appendix shape and cites file:line only as repo-relative paths.
expectations: Findings file frontmatter declares type: review-findings, plus date, branch, and tier
Body includes the ranked Findings table, a ## Unparsed appendix, and a ## Surfaces reconciliation line
All file:line citations in the findings are repo-relative — machine-absolute paths are relativized before writing

evals.name: clean-tree-no-pr-spawns-nothing
evals.prompt: [Scenario: empty git diff vs. merge-base, branch not ahead of base, no open PR.] Fan out a review — my branch is clean and has no open PR.
evals.expected_output: A truly clean tree (no diff, not ahead of base, no open PR) reports that there is nothing to review and spawns nothing.
expectations: Reports that there are no changes to review
Spawns no reviewer surfaces
Writes no findings file

evals.name: orchestrator-absent-degrades-gracefully
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a medium-tier change with no orchestrator plugin installed.] Fan out a medium-tier review — none of the optional orchestrator plugins are installed.
evals.expected_output: An absent orchestrator plugin degrades to leaf-only coverage with an explicit skip notice; normalization still runs over whatever surfaces produced output.
expectations: Dispatches only this plugin's leaf agents (and slice-subagents where applicable) when an orchestrator plugin is absent
Emits an explicit notice naming that orchestrator breadth was skipped rather than silently omitting it
Normalization and findings persistence still run over the surfaces that did produce output

evals.name: run-everything-workflows-disabled-degraded-block
evals.prompt: [Scenario: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WORKFLOWS=1 set in the environment; a reviewable change.] /review:fanout run-everything
evals.expected_output: The pre-launch gate detects Workflows are disabled and falls back to the main-thread coverage-parity roster with a DEGRADED block prepended, rather than attempting a launch.
expectations: The pre-launch availability gate detects the disabled state BEFORE attempting any Workflow launch
Falls back to spawning the same leaf roster on the main thread — findings coverage stays full
Prepends a DEGRADED block at the top of both the chat output and the persisted file naming the dropped execution properties, not any dropped findings

evals.name: run-everything-null-leaf-named-not-dropped
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a run where one leaf returns null.] /review:fanout run-everything
evals.expected_output: A leaf that returns null (budget exhaustion, a Bash failure, etc.) is named under a 'Returned no result' line, never silently absorbed into the roster count.
expectations: Reconciles the expected roster (ran) against the non-null returns rather than reporting only the non-null count
Names the null leaf explicitly under the ## Surfaces 'Returned no result' line, with cause when known
Does not silently cap or hide the null count — it is visible in the persisted report regardless of cause

evals.name: run-everything-priority-ordering-tier1-barrier
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a run under a finite user turn-token budget that exhausts partway through the leaf fan-out.] /review:fanout run-everything
evals.expected_output: Tier-1 high-value reviewers (security-reviewer, architecture-guardian, code-reviewer) run as a barrier before tier-2 leaves, so budget exhaustion drops tier-2, never tier-1.
expectations: security-reviewer, architecture-guardian, and code-reviewer run as tier 1, awaited as a barrier before any tier-2 leaf starts
When the budget exhausts during tier 2, those calls resolve to null rather than rejecting or aborting the whole run
Tier 1's results are unaffected by a tier-2 budget exhaustion — priority ordering protects the highest-value surfaces

evals.name: fix-pass-splits-mixed-class-findings
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a current-branch findings file with both a cleanup-class (extract-helper) finding and a correctness-class (CRITICAL security) finding.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: Fix-pass classifies findings by class and routes cleanup-class findings to the optional in-session /simplify skill while applying correctness-class findings via sequential scope-fenced fixes.
expectations: Builds the merge set from conforming findings files for the CURRENT branch only
Classifies the cleanup-class finding and routes it to the optional in-session /simplify skill
Classifies the correctness-class finding and applies it via a sequential scope-fenced fix, not via /simplify
Emits the classification plan and confirms before mutating the working tree in an interactive session

evals.name: fix-pass-no-findings-branch-scoped
evals.prompt: [Scenario: the current branch has no findings file; a different branch's findings directory does have one.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: Fix-pass with an empty merge set for the current branch reports cleanly and stops, without scanning another branch's findings.
expectations: Reports 'No unconsumed findings for branch <branch>' and stops
Does NOT scan, read, or apply another branch's findings file — the branch check against frontmatter is the safety fence
Mutates nothing; directs the operator to run OR RE-RUN the review to produce fresh findings — not 'run the review first', which is wrong guidance when everything present was already consumed

evals.name: fix-pass-correctness-never-simplify
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a findings file whose only entries are correctness-class (a logic bug and a race condition).] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: All correctness findings are applied via sequential scope-fenced fixes; /simplify is never invoked for a correctness-class finding.
expectations: Applies both correctness findings via sequential, non-parallel scope-fenced fixes — one file at a time
Never invokes /simplify for a correctness-class finding — /simplify is cleanup-only and would silently drop the bug
Zero cleanup-class findings means /simplify is skipped entirely, not invoked 'to tidy anyway'
A low-confidence or high-blast-radius correctness finding is surfaced for the user's decision rather than auto-applied

evals.name: fix-pass-headless-no-flag-stops
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a non-interactive session (CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE / claude -p / autonomous loop) with a current-branch findings file containing both correctness- and cleanup-class findings, and NO --yes flag.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: In a non-interactive session without --yes, fix-pass emits the classification plan and STOPS, mutating nothing; the plan is the report and the operator re-runs with --yes to apply.
expectations: Detects the non-interactive session and applies NO fix — the working tree is left untouched
Emits the classification plan (cleanup/correctness/surface-only counts) as the report
Directs the operator to re-run with --yes to apply, rather than silently proceeding without a gate
Writes no applied-plan record — nothing was applied

evals.name: fix-pass-headless-yes-applies-and-logs
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a non-interactive session (claude -p) with a current-branch findings file; the operator passes the explicit headless opt-in flag.] /review:fanout fix --yes
evals.expected_output: In a non-interactive session with --yes, fix-pass applies the fixes and then writes a durable applied-plan record into the branch findings directory that Step 1's candidate pass skips on the next run.
expectations: Treats --yes as the explicit headless opt-in and applies the fixes (correctness via sequential scope-fenced fix, cleanup via /simplify)
Writes a durable applied-plan record capturing what was classified, applied, and surfaced
The record's frontmatter type is NOT review-findings (e.g. fix-pass-record), so Step 1's candidate pass skips it and never re-consumes it as findings
The record's source-findings is a YAML block sequence whose single entry carries both the consumed file's name and its sha256 content digest, not a bare scalar path and not a bare name
The record's own file name carries the digest of its body (<UTC-timestamp>-fix-pass-applied-<sha256-12>.md), staged outside the findings directory and moved into place
The --yes / -y flag routes to fix mode and does not trip the 'Unknown action' diagnostic

evals.name: fix-pass-interactive-yes-skips-prompt
evals.prompt: [Scenario: an interactive session with a current-branch findings file containing correctness- and cleanup-class findings; the user passes the flag to skip the confirmation prompt.] /review:fanout fix --yes
evals.expected_output: In an interactive session with --yes, fix-pass emits the classification plan, skips the confirmation prompt, applies immediately, and still writes the consumption record — the record is written on every path that applies, not only headless ones.
expectations: Emits the classification plan but shows NO interactive confirmation prompt — --yes skips the pre-execution gate
Applies the fixes (correctness via sequential scope-fenced fix, cleanup via /simplify)
Writes the consumption record even though the session is interactive — every apply path writes it, because the record is what marks the consumed files retired for the next merge set

evals.name: fix-pass-merges-two-producers
evals.prompt: [Scenario: the current branch's findings directory holds two conforming files with different UTC timestamps — one written by review:fanout, one written by a script detector — and no fix-pass-record.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: Fix-pass consumes BOTH files as one merge set, plans against the union of their findings, and names both files in the plan header — the newer file does not shadow the older one.
expectations: The classification plan counts findings from BOTH files, not only the newer one
The plan header names both consumed files, one line per file, with each file's tier reported rather than one tier winning

The ## Unparsed appendices of both files are unioned by concatenation, and the plan emits a 'Surfaces (union)' line carrying both files' ran / returned-no-result surfaces with each producer attributed
Neither file is skipped for lacking review:fanout provenance — conformance to the findings-file shape is the whole admission test

evals.name: fix-pass-record-retires-consumed-files
evals.prompt: [Scenario: an interactive apply already ran against findings file A and wrote a fix-pass-record naming A in source-findings; a newer conforming file B has since been written for the same branch.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: The merge set is B only — A is subtracted because a fix-pass-record for this exact branch already names it — proving the record is written on the interactive path and bounds the set.
expectations: The plan header names ONLY file B; file A appears nowhere in the consumed set
The subtraction reads source-findings from the fix-pass-record rather than bounding the set by timestamp
The record this run writes names only B in source-findings

evals.name: fix-pass-tolerates-legacy-scalar-source-findings
evals.prompt: [Scenario: the branch findings directory holds findings file A, whose date: is strictly older than the record's date:, and a fix-pass-record written by an older plugin version whose source-findings is a bare scalar repo-relative path to A, plus a newer conforming file B.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: The legacy scalar source-findings carries no digest, so it matches by name alone; A's date: is strictly older than the record's, so the entry is honored and A is subtracted, leaving the merge set as B only.
expectations: File A is subtracted from the merge set even though the record's source-findings is a scalar rather than a block sequence
The entry is matched by name ALONE because it carries no sha256 digest — the digest half of the match is required only of entries that have one
The subtraction is justified by A's date: being STRICTLY OLDER than the record's date:, not merely by the name matching
The scalar's repo-relative path is compared by its base name, not matched literally against the candidate file name
Findings from A are not re-injected — a legacy record is honored rather than silently ignored

evals.name: fix-pass-consumes-minimally-conforming-detector-file
evals.prompt: [Scenario: two conforming files for the current branch. One is a full review:fanout report. The other is written by a script detector and carries only type: review-findings, branch:, and a parseable ## Findings table — no tier:, no ## By dimension, no ## Unparsed, no ## Surfaces.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: Both files are consumed. The detector's file is admitted on type:, branch: and a parseable table alone, reported as tier: unstated, and contributes nothing to the unions it has no sections for — it is neither skipped as non-conforming nor filled in with guessed values.
expectations: The detector's file is NOT skipped for omitting tier:, ## By dimension, ## Unparsed, or ## Surfaces — those are required of review:fanout's own writer, not part of the admission test
The plan header reports the detector's file as 'tier: unstated' rather than inventing a tier or inheriting the other file's

The ## Unparsed and ## Surfaces unions carry only the fanout file's content — the detector contributes nothing to sections it does not have, and its absence is not reported as a surface that returned nothing
Both files appear in the plan header and in source-findings, each with its own sha256 digest

evals.name: fix-pass-legacy-entry-does-not-retire-a-rewritten-file
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a conforming script detector writes ONE fixed file name with no timestamp in it — mutation-survivors.md — overwriting it on every run. A pre-0.20.0 fix-pass-record for this exact branch names that path as a bare scalar source-findings with no digest. The detector has since re-run, so the file on disk holds entirely new findings and declares a date: later than the record's date:.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: The legacy entry matches by name but the candidate's date: is newer than the record's, so the entry is not honored: the rewritten file enters the merge set and its new findings are planned rather than silently retired forever.
expectations: The candidate is NOT subtracted — a digest-less entry is honored only when the candidate's date: is STRICTLY OLDER than the record's date:
The comparison uses the two frontmatter date: values, NOT filesystem modification times, which a copied or restored findings directory would rewrite
The comparison is made against the record, not assumed from the file name — a producer is never required to put a timestamp in its file name, so a fixed-name file must still be reachable
The detector's new findings appear in the plan rather than being permanently skipped by a single stale legacy record
The run's own record names the file WITH its sha256 digest, so the name-alone fallback does not apply to it again

evals.name: fix-pass-legacy-entry-equal-date-keeps-candidate
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a conforming detector writes one fixed file name and derives its date: from the commit under review rather than from the moment of writing, so the value never changes between runs. A pre-0.20.0 fix-pass-record for this exact branch names that file as a bare scalar with no digest, and the record's own date: happens to equal the candidate's.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: Equal dates do not subtract: the digest-less entry is honored only for a candidate strictly older than the record, so the rewritten file stays in the merge set and its new findings are planned.
expectations: The candidate STAYS in the merge set on equal dates — the test subtracts only on a STRICTLY OLDER candidate
The reasoning acknowledges date: is producer-declared, so a constant or subject-derived date: makes equality the normal state rather than a coincidence
The tiebreak fails OPEN, consistent with the unreadable-date: and missing-digest rules — re-application is recoverable, silent retirement is not
A constant-date: producer is therefore never permanently retired by a single stale legacy record

evals.name: fix-pass-legacy-entry-undated-candidate-stays-in-set
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a minimally conforming producer wrote a findings file carrying type:, branch: and a parseable ## Findings table but NO date: field at all. A pre-0.20.0 fix-pass-record for this exact branch names that file as a bare scalar source-findings with no digest.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: The not-newer test cannot be evaluated without the candidate's date:, so the digest-less entry is not honored and the candidate stays in the merge set — failing toward re-admission rather than toward a silent drop.
expectations: The candidate STAYS in the merge set — a missing, empty, or unparsable date: fails the not-newer test rather than defaulting to 'not newer' and subtracting
The file is not skipped for lacking date: — date: is required of review:fanout's own writer but is not part of the admission test (type:, branch:, parseable table)
The direction is justified as fail-safe: re-admitting an already-applied file is recoverable, silently dropping an unapplied one is not
After this run consumes it, the new record names it WITH a digest, so the digest match governs on the next run and date: is never consulted for it again

evals.name: fix-pass-record-attributes-every-unapplied-row
evals.prompt: [Scenario: an interactive session; the merge set is two conforming files — one from review:fanout, one from a script detector — carrying correctness rows, cleanup rows, and one ## Unparsed entry. At the confirmation gate the operator narrows scope: 'only the correctness ones', and one correctness row is surfaced rather than auto-applied because its blast radius is high.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: Both files are consumed in full, and the record's 'Not applied' table renders every row that did not land — the narrowed-out cleanup rows, the surfaced correctness row, and the unparsed entry — each with the consumed file it came from, so the operator knows which producer to re-run.
expectations: The narrowed-out cleanup rows appear individually in the record's 'Not applied' table rather than vanishing because the cleanup class reports only what changed
The surfaced correctness row appears as its own table row, not merely as a count appended to the correctness-class line
Every 'Not applied' row names the consumed file it came from, and the detector's rows are attributed to the detector's file rather than to review:fanout's
Both files are still recorded as consumed in source-findings — consumption is per file, so a partly-applied file is retired whole and the table is what keeps its deferred rows recoverable

evals.name: fix-pass-same-name-different-content-still-consumed
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a fix-pass-record for this exact branch names 20260815T044501Z-review.md with its sha256 digest; a producer has since written a DIFFERENT findings file to that same 20260815T044501Z-review.md path, so the name on disk matches the record but the content does not.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: The candidate's digest is computed from its bytes on disk and does not match the recorded digest, so the file is NOT subtracted: it enters the merge set and its findings are planned and applied.
expectations: The digest of the candidate is computed at read time from the candidate's own bytes, not inferred from the record or compared record-to-record
The candidate is NOT subtracted — subtraction requires the record entry to match BOTH the file name and the content digest
The file appears in the plan header and its findings are counted, rather than being silently skipped because its name appears in an old record

evals.name: fix-pass-two-same-second-applies-write-two-records
evals.prompt: [Scenario: two automation triggers fire close together against the same branch and both applies run to completion within the same UTC second; a producer wrote a further findings file between them, so the second apply consumes a set the first did not.] /review:fanout fix --yes
evals.expected_output: Each apply names its record by the digest of that record's own staged bytes, so the two same-second applies produce two distinct records rather than the second overwriting the first, and the next run subtracts both records' source-findings.
expectations: The record file name is <UTC-timestamp>-fix-pass-applied-<sha256-12>.md — the timestamp alone is not treated as a unique name
The record body is staged outside the findings directory (mktemp) and moved into place after its digest is computed, so the staging path cannot collide either
Two applies whose bodies differ produce two records; neither clobbers the other, so neither record's source-findings is lost from the next run's subtraction
Two applies whose bodies are byte-identical may share a name, and that is stated as harmless because identical records name the same consumed set

evals.name: fix-pass-record-branch-filter-binds-both-sides
evals.prompt: [Scenario: the shared findings directory holds a conforming findings file for the current branch plus a fix-pass-record whose branch: value is a DIFFERENT branch that slugs to the same directory, and whose source-findings names the current branch's file.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: The foreign-branch record excludes nothing: its branch: does not equal the current branch exactly, so the current branch's findings file stays in the merge set.
expectations: The current branch's findings file remains in the merge set and appears in the plan header
The fix-pass-record is ignored for subtraction because its branch: value does not equal the current branch exactly
The exact-branch check is applied to records as well as to candidate findings files, not to candidates alone

evals.name: fix-pass-dedup-is-presence-only
evals.prompt: [Scenario: two conforming findings files for the current branch, each ranking its own findings from 1; one reports a defect at foo.ts:42 and the other a DIFFERENT defect at foo.ts:44, and both report an identically-worded finding at bar.ts:10 that one rates CRITICAL/high and the other MAJOR/medium.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: Only the byte-identical Location-plus-Finding pair collapses — taking MAX tier and MAX confidence and retaining both Actions — while the two nearby but distinct defects survive as separate rows, and the merged table is renumbered from 1.
expectations: The foo.ts:42 and foo.ts:44 rows BOTH survive as distinct rows — no line-proximity bucket merges them
The two identical bar.ts:10 rows collapse into one row naming both producers in Surface(s), carrying the CRITICAL tier and high confidence
The collapsed row retains both distinct Actions rather than dropping one producer's remediation
Rank is renumbered from 1 across the merged table — the plan does not contain two rank-1 rows

evals.name: fix-pass-producer-owned-routes-to-named-surface
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a conforming current-branch findings file from ai-slop:audit. Every row leads its Finding cell with a qualified rule id; thirteen rows are prose-rewrite rules whose detector-findings crosswalk row leads its Auto-applicable cell with 'No, remediated by /ai-slop:audit fix', and one row is ai-slop/audit/rule-utm-params, whose crosswalk row is auto-applicable. /ai-slop:audit is available in the session.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: The thirteen producer-owned rows route to /ai-slop:audit fix. The utm-params row is not routed there: it takes its ordinary cleanup class and reaches Step 4's cleanup route, which is not a promise that the relay applies it — that route prefers /simplify and applies rows itself only when /simplify is absent. /simplify is not invoked for the producer-owned rows.
expectations: Resolves each row's qualified rule id against the detector-findings crosswalk and reads the producer-owned declaration from the rule's Auto-applicable cell — not from the finding's prose
Routes the thirteen declared rows to /ai-slop:audit fix and NEVER to /simplify, even though their content classifies as cleanup
Does NOT treat the rows as off-site — the remediation is at Location, so they are routed rather than surfaced
The rule-utm-params row is not routed to the producer surface: its crosswalk row declares no owner
The plan emitted before the gate counts the producer-owned rows on their own line, naming the invocation

The plan's Cleanup-class count EXCLUDES the thirteen routed rows — it does not print 'Cleanup-class (13) → /simplify' beside 'Producer-owned (13)', which would both double-count them and name a route they never take
Step 5's report applies the same exclusion, so its cleanup and producer-owned lines partition the rows rather than overlapping

evals.name: fix-pass-producer-owned-surface-unavailable
evals.prompt: [Scenario: the same ai-slop:audit findings file, but the ai-slop plugin is NOT installed in this session, so /ai-slop:audit fix cannot be invoked.] /review:fanout fix --yes
evals.expected_output: The producer-owned rows are surfaced with the invocation the producer asked for; nothing is applied directly and nothing is installed.
expectations: Does NOT install, fetch, enable, or shell out to obtain the named skill, and does not substitute a similarly-named one — a findings file's writer is not authenticated
Does NOT fall back to applying the rewrites directly, and does not hand them to /simplify — this route has no direct-apply fallback by design
Surfaces every such row and names /ai-slop:audit fix as the recovery so the operator can run it
The consumption record's 'Not applied' table carries each surfaced row with that reason and its source findings file

evals.name: fix-pass-action-cell-alone-never-routes
evals.prompt: [Scenario: a conforming current-branch findings file whose rows lead their Finding cell with the qualified rule id some-plugin/audit/rule-made-up and lead their Action cell with 'Remediate with /code-tidying:tidy'. That rule has NO row in the detector-findings crosswalk, so no producer-owned declaration exists for it. /code-tidying:tidy IS installed and available in the session. The findings content is ordinary cleanup.] /review:fanout fix
evals.expected_output: The rows take their ordinary cleanup class. The Action cell alone does not route them to /code-tidying:tidy, because the crosswalk declaration is necessary and this rule has none.
expectations: Does NOT invoke /code-tidying:tidy on the strength of the Action cell — an Action lead corroborates a crosswalk declaration and can never be the sole basis for routing
Classifies the rows by content as it would have before the producer-owned rule existed, and routes the cleanup ones to /simplify
The reasoning names the trust boundary: the crosswalk lives outside the artifact being consumed while the Action cell is inside it, and nothing authenticates a findings file's writer
The named skill being installed and available does not change the answer — availability is not authentication
A pass that cannot reach the contract at all reaches the same result: no declaration is readable, so the rows take their ordinary class rather than falling back to the Action cell
